title: Identity
description:
Our panel will be discussing how certain concepts are represented in gamesand why they’re represented that way. Each panelist will be covering adifferent aspect of the self and examining how players explore said aspectsin and outside of games.

To start, we will have the audience play a version of HARVL, a socialdeduction game with roleplaying elements. This will contextualize ouridentity-focused presentations.

Esteban will use the affordances of role-playing games to understand whyFacebook’s version of the Metaverse was largely unsuccessful. Though manyRPGs – from tabletop to MMOs – already provide a safe and shared space forpersonal expression, what is the role of technology in creating 'limitless”social worlds?

Mars will examine the Bioshock series to analyze how the heroic fatherprotagonist and the systematic erasure/demonization of motherhood doesnot necessarily celebrate fatherhood — rather, “exceptional” male parenting issimply ordinary maternal expectations rebranded as “heroism”.

Lucas will draw on the principles of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy as a lens toexplore how mental illness can be taught and represented in games withoutthe stigma and horror tied to it. He will develop a framework and apply it toexamine how Depression Quest portrays the struggles of depression notthrough psychological horror imagery, but through its procedural rhetoric.

Despoina/DLC will discuss representation of gender in nonhuman characters and analyze how it leads to gender and identity play in Pokémonfans both in-game and IRL. She will examine cosplay, in particular Pokémoncosplay drag (PokeDrag), as a way in which queer Pokemon fans co-opt and co-createthe identities of these creatures alongside the designers.

We will conclude with a brief Q&A session with all panelists. The audiencewill be asked to allow their HARVL roles to guide how they behave duringthe Q&A!

abstracts.title: Despoina/DLC
abstracts.description:
Pokémon, first released during 1996 in versions Red, Green, and later Blue, isa well-beloved video game and transmedia franchise that has amassed allkinds of fans over its 30-year-and-counting lifetime. This presentation aims to discuss the evolution of gender and identity play among Pokémonfans. To that end, I examine five major design choices that have been madeto dictate how gender is represented in the Pokémon world. These are:

● 1996-Now: The introduction and function of Pokémon gender as amechanic

● 2000/2001: The ability to choose the gender of your player character

● 2013: The ability to customize your character avatar

● 2016-2019: The introduction of the first non-binary Pokémon trainer inPokémon GO

● 2025: The advent of gender-neutral clothing in Pokémon Legends: ZA,Pokémon’s latest main series title

My investigation of these features leads me to observe one way Pokémonfans transition their in-game gender and identity play to the physical world. Irefer to the growing Pokémon cosplay drag (or simply, PokéDrag) scene,found in New York City and other cities with vibrant drag communities.Research done to support this analysis includes interviews with queerPokémon fans, as well as academic writing on cosplay/drag, Pokémon andgender representation in games, and the role of Pokémon fan works. This isall in service of my argument that queer Pokémon fans deepen theirrelationship with the source material and by extension, themselves, byco-opting and co-creating the identities of these non-human characters.

My conference contribution will feature a presentation that functions as ascoped down version of the larger video essay and will conclude with aPokéDrag performance from yours truly to further contextualize my thesis.

abstracts.title: Esteban Romero
abstracts.description:
Esteban Romero

The Metaverse is a vision of a digital universe popularized in 2021 after Facebook rebranded itself and announced it as their next social platform. They claimed that people could do anything together in this digital universe – from business to education. A few years later, the company is downscaling their Reality Labsdivision and their proprietary VR social app, Horizon Worlds, has been called 'dead' by major media outlets. In this work, I will analyze the Metaverse beyond itstechnical challenges to understand its failure as a vision and a culture: a'technofuturistic dream' of a post-racial, hyper-connected, and limitless VRutopia. By comparing this ideal to the worlds of role-playing games, I support thethesis that the metaverse was largely unsuccessful because it was pitched as away for people to perform real-world activities and lacked the social structuresafforded by rules. RPGs, on the contrary, tend to provide a safe and isolated spacefor play, socialization, emergent storytelling, and identity expression. Throughour creativity and capacity for social negotiation, we can use games to transformany social experience into a shared fantasy. This leads me to conclude that a partof Meta’s original vision already exists in the context of RGPs and it can be realizedwithout the need for technology.
